title: Nvidia bought only Side A Directors & Officers insurance. Should you follow their lead?
summary: Nvidia reportedly bought only Side A Directors & Officers Insurance. Here's why that works at Nvidia's scale, but why startups need Sides B and C, too.
body_markdown:
Nvidia has had an eventful few weeks, full of political intrigue, salacious affairs, and the resignation of leather-jacket-clad CEO and face of the AI industry Jensen Huang. So you’d be forgiven for missing a relatively under-the-radar story about Nvidia: its business insurance.


According to[a report in the Financial Times](https://www.ft.com/content/4aba8386-35cc-463b-a79c-a0c85c362c89?syn-25a6b1a6=1) , Nvidia carried[Directors & Officers (D&O) Insurance](https://www.vouch.us/blog/directors-and-officers-insurance) for up to $900 million for its leadership, but none for the company itself. As class action lawsuits began to be proposed by shareholders, some wondered how a company so big and so important could have left itself so exposed.


But what if they weren’t? What if it was a perfectly reasonable choice for Nvidia to make, even if it’s the absolute wrong one for your company?


## **Nvidia has what we call “a frankly absurd amount of money”**


Unless you have a balance sheet that could be confused with the GDP of a small country, you should be looking at all three parts of D&O coverage. D&O policies typically have[three parts](https://www.vouch.us/blog/sides-a-b-c-directors-and-officers-insurance) :


- Side A covers directors and officers when the company won’t or can’t indemnify them.
- Side B reimburses the company when it pays to defend or settle claims against its directors and officers.
- Side C covers claims made against the company itself.


According to the FT, Nvidia purchased $900 million of Side A protection but none of Sides B or C. That means its executives and directors – like, say, Huang – have substantial personal protection against certain claims, even while the company itself retains the financial exposure that B and C would have covered.


(And that exposure isn't hypothetical. A shareholder lawsuit filed in November alleges that Huang and Nvidia misled investors about his relationship with a former executive of a Singapore-based Nvidia customer who U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of working for Chinese intelligence.)


Most companies buy all three sides of D&O coverage, but Nvidia isn't most companies.


According to its[July 2026 quarterly filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/000104581026000075/nvda-20260726.htm) , Nvidia held over $56 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and marketable debt securities.[Some estimates put the global D&O market](https://www.6wresearch.com/industry-report/global-directors-and-officers-insurance-market) at around $48 billion. A balance sheet that big changes the insurance calculus. Buying enough Side B and C coverage to meaningfully protect a company of Nvidia’s size would be expensive even for them, and a large policy would still only cover a fraction of the potential exposure.


Instead, it looks like Nvidia made a rational, if counterintuitive, tradeoff: protect its leadership with Side A while retaining much of the company's own D&O liability risk.


"Nvidia's approach is pretty reasonable," says Travis Hedge, co-founder and CEO of Vouch. "They have more cash on their balance sheet than the entire global D&O market writes in premium in a year, so choosing to carry that risk themselves while buying Side A actually makes sense. It’s a common move amongst companies of their scale."


Buying more insurance doesn’t automatically make for better risk management. Most companies aren’t Nvidia, but every company can ask which losses they can afford to absorb and which risks make sense to transfer to an insurer.


## **So, why did Nvidia even have Side A?**


What makes Nvidia's decision even more interesting is that it didn't abandon D&O Insurance entirely. After all, a $900 million policy isn’t small. Why go so big on one leg of the policy and abandon the others? Turns out that also makes sense if you dig a little deeper.


Side A isn't about protecting “Nvidia, the company”, it's about protecting the personal assets of the people running it. If execs face a covered claim that Nvidia can't pay on their behalf, Side A helps keep them from having to pay out of their own pockets. Think of it as CYA insurance.


But even Nvidia's enormous cash reserves can't solve every problem. Like many companies, Nvidia is incorporated in Delaware. And under[Delaware corporate law](https://delcode.delaware.gov/title8/c001/sc04/index.html) , certain shareholder derivative lawsuits, where shareholders sue on behalf of the company, can leave directors and officers personally liable for judgments the company can't legally pay on their behalf. Side A fills that gap.


In other words, while Nvidia might be comfortable betting its own money on its executives' decisions, that doesn't mean executives should have to put their personal fortunes on the line.


## **Your startup isn't Nvidia. Your D&O strategy shouldn't be, either**


Could Nvidia absorb a substantial company-level D&O claim without jeopardizing its ability to operate? Probably. Could most venture-backed companies? Probably not. Even a claim that ultimately goes nowhere can result in tens or hundreds of thousands in legal expenses.


"The cash you'd use to defend a lawsuit is the same cash you're counting on to hire, launch a product, or move into an office space,” Hedge says. “That's a very different calculation from Nvidia's. You’re gambling with your company’s survival without that safety net."


Directors & Officers claims don't just arise from headline-grabbing espionage and affairs. They can come from the everyday decisions involved in building a company. You raise a round at a lower valuation that creates conflict between existing and new shareholders; an acquisition benefits one class of investors over another; a disagreement over equity dilution, financial disclosures, or the direction of the business turns into allegations of mismanagement.


As a startup grows, it also accumulates more stakeholders with competing interests. Founders, investors, board members, and employees all have different expectations about how the company should run. Decisions that move the business forward can also create grounds for a dispute. Sides B and C can help protect the company against covered claims arising from those decisions, not just allegations against individual directors.


In Vouch advisors' conversations with startup founders, requests for D&O Insurance usually come from an investor or incoming independent director who wants protection for their personal assets. That's what Side A is for. But protecting your directors isn't the same as protecting your company. Sides B and C help ensure that defending leadership decisions or the company itself doesn't come at the expense of the business you're trying to build.


For most startups, the appropriate starting point for D&O is a program that includes all three sides, with limits and retentions suited to your stage, capital raised, board composition, and potential liabilities. Investor requirements and indemnification agreements should also inform the decision.


## **Get a D&O program that’s more tailored than a leather jacket**


Nvidia's approach is reasonable because of its extraordinary financial resources and its capacity to retain losses that could threaten a smaller business.


That doesn't mean every company should follow Nvidia's lead and start dropping coverage. It also doesn’t mean buying the largest policy available.


What founders can learn from Nvidia is the importance of being deliberate about risk. What matters is understanding which losses your own company could realistically absorb and which could put its future at risk.
